passages.text: I signed up to volunteer at a food bank last January, mostly because my New Year's resolution list was looking embarrassingly short. I expected to spend a few hours stacking tins and feeling virtuous. What I didn't expect was how much I'd learn about my own neighbourhood. The people who came through the door weren't strangers — they were the woman from the dry cleaner's, the retired teacher from the end of my street. Poverty doesn't announce itself. It sits quietly in the houses you walk past every day. I've been going back every Saturday since.
passages.label: Text 1 — Online Article: Why Everyone Should Try Volunteering

passages.text: My dearest Catherine, I must tell you of the charitable bazaar held at the Assembly Rooms last Thursday. Mrs Alderton had organised the whole affair with her customary thoroughness, and the ladies of the parish had been sewing for weeks. I took charge of the preserves stall, which proved more popular than I had anticipated — every jar was sold within the first hour. The curate gave a short address on the duty of Christian charity, after which the Reverend Mr Fothergill auctioned a painted screen that fetched three guineas. We raised eleven pounds in total, which will go towards blankets for the workhouse. I confess I felt a satisfaction quite beyond what I had expected.
passages.label: Text 2 — Letter to a Friend, 1867

passages.text: Community fridges are appearing on high streets across Britain, and they're changing the way we think about food waste. The concept is simple: restaurants, supermarkets, and households donate surplus food to a shared fridge that anyone can use. No questions asked, no means testing, no stigma. In Manchester, one fridge redistributes over two hundred meals a week. 'People feel differently about taking food when it's framed as reducing waste rather than accepting charity,' says coordinator Priya Okonkwo. The movement has grown from twelve fridges in 2017 to over three hundred today. It suggests that communities, when given the right tools, will organise themselves.
passages.label: Text 3 — Magazine Feature: The Rise of Community Fridges

passages.text: Tuesday 14th October. Rose at six and walked to the schoolhouse before the bell. The children were already gathered in the yard, some without shoes despite the cold. I taught reading from the primer until half past nine, then arithmetic until noon. Mrs Bowen brought soup for those who had no dinner of their own. I am struck, as I often am, by the eagerness of even the youngest children to learn. They have so little, yet they sit with such attention. If only the parish would provide more slates — three children must share one between them, and the chalk wears to nothing by Thursday.
passages.label: Text A — Diary Entry, 1851

passages.text: It is a matter of some considerable disgrace that the streets of this city remain in so deplorable a condition. The Corporation has seen fit to raise the rates by sixpence in the pound, yet the gutters of Bridewell Lane run with refuse and the pavements of Market Street are cracked beyond safe use. We have written to the Mayor on no fewer than three occasions. Each time we have received assurances that improvements are forthcoming. Each time, nothing has changed. The ratepayers of this city deserve better than promises. They deserve drains that function, pavements that do not imperil the elderly, and an administration that treats public money as a trust, not a convenience.
passages.label: Text B — Newspaper Editorial, 1874

passages.text: Ladies and gentlemen, I stand before you this evening to speak of a matter that ought to trouble the conscience of every person in this room. In the courts and alleys not half a mile from where we sit, families of eight and ten share a single room. The children sleep on straw. The water is drawn from a pump that serves forty households and has not been inspected in a twelvemonth. I do not say these things to distress you. I say them because ignorance is the friend of inaction, and inaction is the enemy of the poor. We have the means to improve these lives. The question is whether we have the will.
passages.label: Text C — Speech to a Philanthropic Society, 1889

passages.text: I used to buy a new outfit every weekend. Seriously — every single weekend. Then one day I watched a documentary about garment workers in Bangladesh and I couldn't unzip my new jacket without feeling sick. So I stopped. Cold turkey. No new clothes for six months. And you know what? Nobody noticed. Not my friends, not my colleagues, not the barista who definitely judges my shoes. The world kept spinning. My wardrobe didn't shrink — I just started actually wearing the clothes I already owned. I'm not saying everyone needs to go full monk mode. But maybe we could all stand to ask ourselves: do I need this, or do I just want the feeling of buying it?
passages.label: Text A — Blog Post: Why I Stopped Buying Fast Fashion

passages.text: Good morning everyone. I want to talk to you today about something that sounds simple but is actually quite radical. Kindness. Not the big, headline-grabbing kind — not charity runs or fundraising galas. I mean the small, invisible kind. Holding a door. Saying thank you like you mean it. Noticing when someone in your class has gone quiet. Last year, a student in this school told a teacher that the only reason they got through a difficult week was because someone sat with them at lunch. That's it. No grand gesture. Just presence. So here's my challenge to every single one of you: before the end of today, do one kind thing that nobody will ever know about. Not for a reward. Not for recognition. Just because you can.
passages.label: Text B — Speech at a School Assembly: Kindness Costs Nothing

passages.text: We have become a nation obsessed with looking backwards. Every other advert sells us a sepia-tinted version of a past that never actually existed — corner shops where everyone knew your name, summers that lasted forever, communities bound together by unspecified but apparently limitless goodwill. The trouble with nostalgia is not that it's inaccurate, though it usually is. The trouble is that it makes the present feel like a disappointment by comparison. When we measure today against a golden age we've invented, we stop noticing what's actually good about now. Our schools are better resourced, our medicine more advanced, our access to information unprecedented. But none of that fits neatly into a sepia filter. Progress doesn't photograph well.
passages.label: Text C — Opinion Column: The Problem with Nostalgia

passages.text: A growing number of parents are choosing to drive their children to school, even when they live within walking distance. The charity Living Streets reports that only 44% of primary school children now walk to school, down from 72% in the 1970s. The consequences are visible every morning: congested roads, double-parked cars, and children who arrive without having taken a single breath of fresh air. Walking gives children independence, exercise, and time to talk with friends. It also teaches them to navigate their environment — a skill they will need long after they leave the school gates.

passages.text: Gentlemen, I write to you concerning the welfare of the children in the parish of Ashford who walk daily to the school at Millbrook, a distance of some two and a half miles. The road passes through open country and is wholly unlit. In the winter months the children must set out before dawn and return after dark. Several have arrived at school soaked through, and one boy last week fell into the ditch beside Langton Bridge and had to be carried the remaining distance by an older pupil. I would respectfully suggest that the Board consider the provision of a covered cart, to be shared among the outlying parishes. The cost would be modest, and the benefit to the children's health and attendance considerable.
passages.label: Text B — Letter to a School Board, 1882

passages.text: She's ten. She asked if she could walk home from school by herself. Every cell in my body screamed no. But I said yes. I watched her disappear round the corner with her rucksack bouncing and I stood there like an idiot, holding my car keys, wondering whether I'd just made a terrible mistake. She was home in eleven minutes. She burst through the door grinning and said, 'I saw a cat and two pigeons and the man at the chip shop waved at me.' That was it. The whole report. No drama, no danger, no stranger lurking behind a hedge. Just a child walking through her own neighbourhood, noticing things, being alive in the world. I'm still terrified. But I'm going to let her do it again tomorrow.
passages.label: Text C — Blog Post: My Daughter's First Walk Home Alone

passages.text: The field behind Ashworth Primary has been a playground, a wildlife corridor, and a breathing space for three decades. Now the council wants to cover it in concrete and call it progress. They plan to build a car park — not a school, not a hospital, not even affordable housing — but a car park. Two hundred and forty parking spaces where children once flew kites and foxes raised their cubs. The trees that line the southern boundary are over fifty years old. You cannot replace fifty years of growth with a sapling and a press release.
passages.label: Text A — Campaign Article: Save Our Green Spaces

passages.text: The condition of the dwellings in Croker's Yard beggars description. We found twelve persons occupying a single room of no more than fourteen feet square. The walls were black with damp and the ceiling so low that a man of ordinary height could not stand fully upright. The only window had been stuffed with rags to keep out the draught, admitting neither light nor air. A child of perhaps four years sat on the floor, gnawing at a crust that appeared to be her only sustenance. The stench was oppressive and did not diminish even after we had been inside some minutes. One is compelled to ask how a civilised society permits such conditions to endure.
passages.label: Text B — Extract from a Victorian Social Report, 1871

passages.text: The cold was the first thing. In Damascus we had sunshine nine months of the year, and even winter was just cool enough for a jacket. Here, the cold came through the walls. It got into my bones. My daughter kept asking why the sky was always the same colour — this flat, heavy grey that sat on the rooftops like a lid. I remember standing in a supermarket for the first time, just staring at the shelves. Not because of the choice, though there was plenty of that. Because it was warm. I stood there for twenty minutes, pretending to read cereal boxes, just to stay warm. That's what no one tells you about being a refugee. It's not just the big losses. It's the small ones — heat, light, the sound of your own language in the street.
passages.label: Text C — Magazine Interview: A Refugee's First Winter in Britain

steps.content: The writer juxtaposes 'two hundred and forty parking spaces' with 'children once flew kites and foxes raised their cubs.' The number is cold and industrial; the imagery is warm and living.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: The writer uses juxtaposition to contrast the sterile reality of 'two hundred and forty parking spaces' with the living imagery of 'children once flew kites and foxes raised their cubs.' The numerical precision makes the car park feel cold and bureaucratic, while the natural imagery appeals to emotion. The word 'once' shifts the field into past tense, making the loss feel imminent and irreversible.

passages.text: Picture this: a high street where children play in the road. Where the only sound is conversation, birdsong, and the occasional clatter of a delivery bicycle. It sounds like a fantasy. But in the Dutch town of Houten, it has been reality since the 1980s. Cars are not banned entirely — residents can still drive to their homes — but through-traffic is routed around the town centre, not through it. The result is striking. Accident rates have dropped by over sixty per cent. Air quality has improved measurably. Property prices have risen. And something harder to quantify: people say they talk to their neighbours more. The critics said it would kill business. It didn't. The town centre is thriving, precisely because people want to spend time there. Houten didn't ban cars to punish drivers. It redesigned its streets to put people first.
passages.label: Text A — Article: The Town That Banned Cars

passages.text: I entered the women's ward at half past two. The corridor was narrow and unlit, and the air carried a sour, stale odour that clung to my clothes long after I had left. The first cell I visited held a woman of perhaps thirty, though she appeared far older. She sat on a wooden bench with her hands in her lap and did not raise her eyes when I entered. In the second cell, two women shared a space barely large enough for one. They had been given a single blanket between them. I asked the warder how long these women had been confined. He told me the first had served eight months for theft of a loaf of bread. The second pair had been there since November — nearly five months — awaiting trial. I left the prison at four o'clock. The sunlight outside felt like a different country.
passages.label: Text B — Extract from a Prison Reformer's Journal, 1863

passages.text: I was nineteen the first time I failed at something that mattered. I had applied for a place on a journalism programme and been rejected. The letter was one sentence long. It didn't explain why. I assumed it was because I wasn't good enough, and I carried that assumption around with me for the next three years like a stone in my pocket. Now, I could tell you that failure made me stronger. That's the story we like to tell, isn't it? The tidy narrative where rejection becomes motivation, where every setback has a silver lining stitched in by hindsight. But that's not what happened. What happened was slower and messier. I stopped writing for a year. I applied for jobs I didn't want. I got angry at people who hadn't done anything wrong. And then, gradually, I started again. Not because I'd learned some grand lesson, but because writing was the only thing I was any good at. I tell you this not because my failure was special. I tell you this because yours won't be either. And that's the point.
passages.label: Text C — Speech Transcript: Why We Need to Talk About Failure

method_card.title: Analysing Structural Features
method_card.content: Non-fiction writers organise their texts deliberately. Structure includes how the text opens and closes, how ideas are ordered, where shifts in focus occur, and how the writer guides the reader through the argument or narrative. Analysing structure means explaining why the writer arranged the text this way.

exam_context.frequency: Structure analysis features on every Component 2 paper. Strong answers discuss how structure creates effects, not just what order things happen in.

passages.text: School trips are supposed to enrich learning, but for many families they have become a source of anxiety. A residential trip to an outdoor centre can cost over three hundred pounds per child. Schools insist the trips are 'voluntary contributions', but parents report feeling pressured — their children don't want to be the only ones left behind. A survey by the Child Poverty Action Group found that one in five parents had borrowed money to cover the cost of a school trip. Others send their children with packed lunches while classmates eat at restaurants. The gap between what schools expect and what families can afford has never been wider.
passages.label: Text A — Article: The Hidden Cost of School Trips

passages.text: Dear Mrs Lovell, I write to inform you that the school will arrange an excursion to the coast on the twenty-third of July. The omnibus will depart at seven o'clock in the morning and return before nightfall. Each child is asked to bring a packed luncheon and a shilling for the hiring of bathing machines, should they wish to bathe. I appreciate that a shilling is no trifling sum for some households. Any child whose family cannot meet the cost will be accommodated from the school fund without embarrassment or distinction. It is my firm belief that every child in this school deserves to see the sea, regardless of their father's income. Please confirm your daughter's attendance at your earliest convenience. Yours sincerely, Miss E. Hargreaves.
passages.label: Text B — Letter from a Headmistress, 1897

passages.text: He came home with the letter on a Tuesday. Three hundred and twenty pounds for four nights in the Lake District. I read it twice, then put it on the fridge with a magnet and tried not to think about it. By Friday he'd stopped asking. He'd worked it out for himself. He's eleven. He shouldn't have to read his mother's face to know the answer is no. On the day the coach left, I drove him to school as normal. He didn't cry. He walked in with his rucksack and his lunchbox and he said, 'It's fine, Mum.' But I saw him look at the coach in the car park, and I saw him look away. That's what I can't forget. Not the cost. The look.
passages.label: Text C — Blog Post: When My Son Couldn't Go on the Trip

passages.text: I cleared out my wardrobe last weekend and filled three bin bags for the charity shop. Most of the clothes were barely worn — impulse buys from online sales, items that looked nothing like the photos, things I convinced myself I needed at two in the morning. The average British person buys sixty new garments a year and keeps each one for roughly three years. The factories that produce them operate around the clock in countries most of us could not find on a map. I am not pretending I have the answer, but standing in my bedroom surrounded by three bags of clothes I never needed felt like a symptom of something deeply wrong.
passages.label: Source A — Blog Post: The Problem with Fast Fashion (21st Century)

passages.text: Sir, your recent article on the decline of market stalls missed the point entirely. Markets are not dying because customers have abandoned them — they are dying because councils have priced them out with punishing pitch fees and absurd regulations. My family has run a fruit and vegetable stall at Barton Market for thirty-one years. We know our customers by name. Mrs Hennessy has bought her Sunday apples from us since 1994. The supermarket two streets away cannot offer that. What it can offer is a car park, air conditioning, and prices we cannot match because they buy in quantities we could never dream of. The market is not a relic. It is the last place in this town where you can have a conversation with the person who sells you your dinner.
passages.label: Source B — Letter to a Newspaper: In Defence of Local Markets (21st Century)

passages.text: The trade this quarter has been nothing short of dismal. The railway has brought with it a catalogue firm from Manchester whose prices undercut my own by a margin I cannot hope to match. A bolt of cotton that I sell for three shillings and sixpence arrives by post from their warehouse at two and ninepence, wrapped in brown paper and accompanied by a card promising satisfaction or a full return of the purchase price. My customers are not disloyal — they are practical. Mrs Aldridge, who has bought her linen from this shop for twenty years, showed me the catalogue with something close to guilt on her face. I do not blame her. I blame the world that has decided cheapness matters more than anything else, and I fear for what we lose when the last shop on this street closes its door.
passages.label: Source C — Extract from a Draper's Account, 1871

passages.text: Nobody tells you about the silence. I had expected chaos — thirty teenagers armed with phones and attitude. Instead, when I walked in, they just looked at me. Thirty pairs of eyes, waiting. I introduced myself and wrote my name on the board, and the pen squeaked so loudly in the quiet room that I wanted to disappear. A girl in the front row smiled, and I realised she was trying to put me at ease. A fifteen-year-old, reassuring her teacher. I taught the whole lesson five minutes too fast, ran out of material with ten minutes left, and told them to read quietly. They did. When the bell rang, a boy at the back said, 'See you Thursday, Miss.' It was the kindest thing anyone said to me all day.

passages.text: My daughter brought home her school report last week, and I have been trying to decipher it ever since. She is, according to her English teacher, 'developing her analytical skills with increasing confidence.' Her maths teacher reports that she 'engages well with problem-solving activities when supported.' Her PE teacher says she 'participates with enthusiasm.' None of this tells me whether she can read a novel, solve an equation, or catch a ball. School reports have become a language designed not to communicate but to protect — every sentence carefully calibrated to say nothing that could cause offence, nothing specific enough to be useful, nothing honest enough to require a difficult conversation. My daughter read her report, shrugged, and said, 'They say the same thing about everyone.' She is twelve, and she has already worked out what it took me twenty minutes to decode.

passages.text: Dear Mr Thornton, I write concerning your son Edward, who has now completed his first term at this school. I will not waste your time with pleasantries. The boy cannot sit still for longer than ten minutes. He talks when he should listen, laughs when he should work, and has twice been discovered reading penny dreadfuls behind his Latin grammar. His arithmetic is weak, his handwriting worse, and his Latin would embarrass a child half his age. However — and I say this with some reluctance — he is the most imaginative boy in my class. His compositions, when he can be persuaded to write them, show a mind that sees the world in ways his classmates do not. Last week he compared the fall of Rome to a house with termites, and I confess I have not stopped thinking about it since. He will either distinguish himself or drive me to an early retirement. I have not yet decided which.
passages.label: Source C — Letter from a Schoolmaster to a Parent, 1883

passages.text: I am not a chef. I burn toast with a regularity that my family finds hilarious and I find depressing. But I can feed four people a decent meal for under eight pounds, and I do it most nights. That, in this economy, is not a hobby — it is a survival skill. Schools teach children about Pythagoras and the water cycle but not how to boil an egg. We send eighteen-year-olds to university with a loan, a duvet, and absolutely no idea how to feed themselves. They survive on takeaways and instant noodles until their money runs out, then they ring their parents. I know this because I was one of them. Cooking is not glamorous. It is not Instagram-worthy. But it is the difference between eating well and eating badly, and that difference shapes everything — health, mood, money, independence.
passages.label: Source A — Opinion Column: Why Everyone Should Learn to Cook (21st Century)

passages.text: Let me say something that will make half the teachers in this country reach for their red pens: homework does not work. Study after study has shown that for primary-age children, homework has no measurable impact on achievement. For older students, the gains are modest and often offset by the stress, family conflict, and lost sleep it causes. I watched my ten-year-old son spend forty-five minutes last Tuesday copying out spellings he already knew, while the evening sunshine disappeared behind the houses. He could have been riding his bike, reading a book he actually wanted to read, or simply being a child — which is, I am told, a developmental stage that has a deadline. Instead, he sat at the kitchen table with a pencil in one hand and resentment in the other. Homework exists because we have always done it. That is not a reason. That is a habit.
passages.label: Source B — Newspaper Editorial: The Case Against Homework (21st Century)

passages.text: Sir, I have this week visited the cotton mills of Bradford and seen with my own eyes what no report or statistic can convey. Children of eight and nine years stand at the machines for twelve hours without rest, their fingers raw from the thread, their faces grey with exhaustion. I spoke to one boy, Thomas, who told me he had not attended a school in his life and could not write his own name. His overseer, a man of perhaps thirty, assured me that the children are well treated and that their wages support their families. I do not doubt his sincerity, but I question his judgement. A child who cannot write his name has been taught to operate a machine at the cost of his future. The factories produce cloth. They also produce something else entirely: a generation of citizens who will know how to work but not how to think.
passages.label: Source C — Letter to The Times on Child Labour, 1842

passages.text: I deleted my social media accounts six months ago, and I have not missed them for a single day. I used to spend two hours every evening scrolling through other people's lives — their holidays, their meals, their filtered faces — and feeling quietly worse about my own. My phone screen time dropped from five hours a day to ninety minutes. I started reading again. I slept better. The friends I thought I would lose? The real ones texted me. The rest disappeared, which told me everything I needed to know. Social media is not connection. It is a performance of connection, and I was both the audience and the actor, and I was exhausted by both roles.
passages.label: Source A — Blog Post: Why I Deleted Social Media (21st Century)

passages.text: I am writing in response to your article about the dangers of social media. I have a chronic illness that keeps me housebound for weeks at a time. During my worst episodes, social media is the only thing that connects me to other human beings. I found a support group for my condition on an online forum, and the people in it understand what I am going through in a way that even my closest family cannot. When I was in hospital last year, a woman from that group sent me a card. I have never met her in person, but she knew my medication, my fears, and my sense of humour. That is real connection. Dismissing social media as toxic ignores the millions of people for whom it is a lifeline — not a luxury, but the only form of community available to them.
passages.label: Source B — Letter to a Magazine: Social Media Saved My Life (21st Century)

passages.text: The penny post has been in operation for fourteen years, and its effects on the character of this nation are now plain to see. Where once a letter was a considered thing — composed with care, sealed with thought, sent only when the matter was of genuine importance — the post now carries trivial correspondence by the sack-load. Gentlemen write to arrange luncheon. Ladies write to describe their hats. The ease and cheapness of communication has not elevated the quality of what is communicated; it has, if anything, diminished it. I do not wish to seem ungrateful for the convenience, but I observe that when everything can be said, much is said that need not be. The art of silence — of choosing what is worth committing to paper — is, I fear, being lost, and with it a certain quality of attention that our grandchildren may never know.
passages.label: Source C — Essay on the Effects of the Penny Post, 1854

passages.text: A library is not a building full of books. It is a building full of doors. Every shelf is a corridor, every spine a threshold, and the quiet hum of turning pages is the sound of people deciding who they want to become. I grew up in a house without books. My parents worked long hours and read nothing but bills. The library on Marsh Road was my escape, my education, and eventually my ambition. The librarian, Mrs Okoro, never asked me what I was doing there. She just pointed me towards the next shelf. Closing a library is not saving money. It is locking a door and pretending nobody needed to walk through it.
passages.label: Source A — Speech: The Importance of Libraries (21st Century)

passages.text: I understand the nostalgia. I really do. Libraries are lovely. They smell nice. They have kind volunteers and those satisfying rubber stamps. But we have to be honest: the library as we knew it is finished. The internet has made more information available to more people than every library in this country combined. A child in a tower block can access the British Library's entire digital archive from a phone. The argument that libraries serve disadvantaged communities would hold more weight if those communities actually used them. Footfall in public libraries has dropped by forty per cent in a decade. You cannot keep a building open because it was useful thirty years ago. That is not policy. That is sentimentality dressed up as principle.
passages.label: Source B — Newspaper Column: Who Needs Libraries When We Have the Internet? (21st Century)

passages.text: Gentlemen, you have before you this evening a modest collection of volumes — three hundred and twelve, to be precise — which your subscriptions have purchased over the past year. They are not much to look at. The shelves are plain deal, the bindings are cheap, and several of the books have already been read so often that their spines are cracked and their pages loose. But I would ask you to consider what these books represent. A cotton weaver who reads a book of natural philosophy is no longer merely a weaver. He is a man who understands the machinery he operates. A clerk who reads history is no longer merely a clerk. He is a citizen who comprehends the forces that have shaped his world. Knowledge does not care who holds it. It transforms whoever is willing to reach for it.
passages.label: Source C — Address to the Mechanics' Institute, 1847

passages.text: Ladies and gentlemen, let me ask you a question. When did we decide that a car park was more important than a place where children can play? Riverside Park has been the heart of this community for eighty years. Your grandparents walked there. Your children play there. And now the council wants to cover it in tarmac because a supermarket chain has offered them money. This is not progress. This is vandalism with planning permission. I urge you — every one of you — to sign this petition, attend the meeting on Thursday, and tell the council that this park is not for sale.

passages.text: I had expected something fierce — jagged peaks, howling wind, the kind of landscape that punishes you for showing up unprepared. What I found was gentler than that. The hills rolled rather than jutted. The lochs lay flat and silver, reflecting clouds that moved so slowly they seemed to be resting. On the third day I walked twelve miles along a track that followed a river through a valley of birch trees, and I did not see another person for five hours. The silence was not empty. It was full — of water, of wind in leaves, of something I can only describe as the sound of the land breathing. I sat on a rock, ate a sandwich, and wondered why I had ever thought I needed to be anywhere else.

We work fourteen hours in the mills for wages that scarcely purchase bread. Our children are born into rooms without light and grow in streets without drainage. We ask not for charity but for justice. We do not beg — we demand that the laws of this country recognise us as men and not as machinery. Let the gentlemen of Parliament walk one week in our shoes, breathe the air of our factories, and drink the water of our wells, and we believe their votes would change before their shoes dried.

passages.text: I sat in a restaurant last week and counted. Of the fourteen tables around me, eleven had at least one person looking at a phone. A couple opposite sat in complete silence for twenty minutes, each scrolling through their own screen. When their food arrived, they both took photographs of it. Then they went back to their phones. I wanted to lean over and say something — I am not sure what, exactly — but the moment felt too absurd for intervention. We have built a world in which we can reach anyone, anywhere, at any time, and the result is that we no longer speak to the person sitting opposite us. The technology that promised to connect us has achieved the precise opposite. We are more networked than any generation in human history, and we are lonelier. My grandmother, who had no phone, no email, and no internet, spoke to her neighbours every day. She knew their children's names, their illnesses, their worries. I have four hundred followers on social media. I could not name a single one of them.
passages.label: Source A — Magazine Feature: The Death of Conversation (21st Century)

passages.text: There was a time, not so very distant, when the arrival of a letter was an event of genuine consequence. The postman's knock would bring the household to the hallway, and the breaking of a seal carried with it a mixture of anticipation and dread, for a letter might contain news of a birth, a death, a fortune, or a disaster. One read carefully, weighed every sentence, and replied with equal deliberation. A letter was composed, not dashed off. It was a considered act of communication, shaped by the knowledge that one's words would be held, re-read, and perhaps preserved for years. I fear this art is declining. The penny post, for all its democratic virtues, has made correspondence so cheap and so easy that we write without thinking, send without caring, and discard without remembering. The letter that once carried weight now carries only habit. And when everything is written, nothing, I suspect, is truly said.
passages.label: Source B — Essay on the Art of Letter Writing, 1862

passages.text: November the fourteenth. The storm has been blowing for three days now and shows no sign of easing. I have not seen another living soul since Monday, when the supply boat was turned back by the swell. The lamp requires tending every four hours, and between times I read, or write, or simply sit and listen to the wind finding new ways to sound angry. I received a letter from my wife last week — she writes that the children are well, that the roof has been mended, and that the cat has learned to open the larder door. I have read it eleven times. Not because the news is remarkable, but because her handwriting is the closest thing I have to her voice. The words are ordinary. But they arrive from a world I cannot reach, carried by a boat across water I cannot cross, and each time I unfold the paper it is as if she has walked into the room.
passages.label: Source C — Diary Entry of a Lighthouse Keeper, 1891

worked_examples.question: List four things you learn about modern communication from Source A.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.content: Ideas: Both writers argue that easier communication has reduced its quality. Source A: phones have replaced conversation ('we no longer speak to the person sitting opposite us'). Source B: cheap postage has replaced careful letters ('we write without thinking').

steps.label: Step 2
steps.content: Methods: Source A uses observational anecdote (the restaurant scene) and statistics (four hundred followers, zero named). Source B uses contrast between past and present ('composed, not dashed off') and a formal, reflective register.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.content: Tone: Source A is wry and frustrated. Source B is elegiac and philosophical. Both end with powerful paradoxes: Source A — 'more networked… and lonelier'; Source B — 'when everything is written, nothing is truly said.'

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: Both writers argue that easier communication diminishes its quality. Source A uses modern observational evidence — the restaurant scene, the four hundred unnamed followers — to show that technology creates loneliness, not connection. Source B contrasts careful Victorian letter-writing with careless modern correspondence. Their methods differ: Source A's tone is wry and anecdotal; Source B's is elegiac and philosophical. Both end with paradoxes that distil their arguments: Source A's 'more networked… and lonelier' and Source B's 'when everything is written, nothing is truly said' are structurally and thematically parallel despite 160 years of separation.

- Mastering (excellent): Clear, concise summary with well-selected key points; brief supporting evidence.

ai_marking_prompts.synthesis:

- Mastering (excellent): Clear synthesis organised by theme with evidence from both sources; identifies connections and contrasts.
- Secure (good): Synthesises with evidence from both sources; some thematic organisation.
- Developing (needs_work): Some synthesis but may treat sources separately.
- Emerging (not_valid): Writes about one source only.

Be encouraging. Respond in JSON: {"quality":"excellent|good|needs_work|not_valid","feedback":"2-3 sentences","improvement":"optional brief tip"}
ai_marking_prompts.evaluation:
You are a GCSE English Language tutor. The student is evaluating which source most effectively conveys its message. Mark their response using these levels:

- Mastering (excellent): Clear evaluative position with specific analysis of language, structure, and emotional effect across multiple sources.
- Secure (good): Evaluates with evidence; some analysis.
- Developing (needs_work): Some evaluation but limited analysis.
- Emerging (not_valid): No genuine evaluation.

Any choice is valid. Respond in JSON: {"quality":"excellent|good|needs_work|not_valid","feedback":"2-3 sentences","improvement":"optional brief tip"}
ai_marking_prompts.full_comparison:
You are a GCSE English Language tutor marking a full Component 2 comparison response. Mark using these levels:

- Mastering (excellent, 13-16 marks): Perceptive comparison of BOTH ideas AND methods; organised by theme with fluid integration of both sources; analyses specific language, structure, and tone; evaluates effectiveness; uses well-selected evidence throughout.
- Secure (good, 9-12 marks): Clear comparison with evidence from both sources; discusses some methods alongside ideas; mostly well-organised.
- Developing (needs_work, 5-8 marks): Some comparison but may focus on ideas without methods, or treat sources separately; limited analysis.
- Emerging (not_valid, 1-4 marks): Minimal comparison; writes about one source or retells content.

Be encouraging but specific. Reward integrated comparison and method-level analysis. Respond in JSON: {"quality":"excellent|good|needs_work|not_valid","feedback":"3-4 sentences with specific strengths and next steps","improvement":"1-2 sentence actionable tip"}
